column2: A renewal read that calls an account at risk for low usage, when quiet usage is what a healthy compliance deployment looks like in that business.
A plan full of activity with no measure, no owner on the customer side and no way to be wrong. A plan that cannot fail never gets achieved.
A monthly review that looks different every time, so nobody can see what changed. The sections skipped first, proof of value and open promises, are the ones that matter most.
Offering training to every account with unused seats, whatever the cause. A stalled rollout, a broken integration and the wrong people holding licenses each need a different fix.
Asking for a reference at renewal. The timing turns a favor into a trade, and the customer learns that agreeing has a price.
A report on the whole book that ends without a decision. A few accounts or one renewal month carry the risk, and nobody sees it until it becomes a cliff.
A week spent on the accounts that asked. Whoever emails loudest is rarely the biggest risk or the biggest value, and the quiet accounts where the danger sits get nothing.
A deck of usage charts for a customer who wanted to know whether the product is worth keeping. The meeting replays dashboards and decides nothing.
A call that goes well, produces a recap and moves nothing. Everyone leaves satisfied, and the next call has the same agenda.
A tidy recap sent to the main contact while the emails that actually move the account stay unwritten.
Finding out your sponsor left when the renewal arrives. The new owner forms a view of your product from someone else's story before you have spoken to them.
It was an acquisition filed as the cause, hiding months of no contact. A postmortem that ends in a category changes nothing.
A list of six things to improve after a call. It is fair and accurate, and nobody can act on it.
A promise made on a call that nobody writes down. Both sides forget it until the customer remembers it at renewal.
Starting from headcount. Divide the accounts by the CSMs, call the result a ratio and describe it as a strategy.
A dashboard full of metrics with no definitions. Two people read the same number differently, and a strong net figure hides a leaking base.
Installing a library of skills and not knowing which one fits the situation in front of you.
Hiring on rapport alone, then finding out in month three that the new CSM cannot read an account or write a clear update.
Handing a new CSM the hardest accounts on day one, with no context and no time to listen first.
The lead dropped into a queue. A CSM passes a real expansion signal, someone with no context works it, the customer gets a cold sales approach, and the CSM never passes another one.
An update written from your side of the glass. The change that affects the customer sits in the middle of a paragraph about your roadmap.
A day planned around the calendar that filled itself. Recaps happen at midnight, prep gets skipped and the one hard task slides to tomorrow.
A customer email checked for tone while its facts go unchecked, so a wrong date or an upgraded maybe reaches the customer.
Going quiet until you have the answer. Silence reads as chaos or concealment, and both are worse than an update with nothing new in it.
The product tour. Fifteen minutes explaining the platform to someone who does not care how it works, ending in a handshake and nothing else.
The deck that dies in an inbox because the champion could not defend slide four when their CFO pushed back.
Chasing the biggest account for an upsell while a smaller one that already asked for more goes unnoticed, or expanding a deployment that is not working.
The account that arrives as a folder, with everything documented and nothing that matters, or the account that leaves with its owner and the promises with it.
Three paragraphs of context and thanks before the news. The customer knew by the second sentence, waited for the rest and trusts the delivery less than the news.
A score that was green the quarter before a churn, offered as the explanation when the green score is the thing that needs explaining.
Can someone please look at this. It names no decision, no deadline and no owner, so it sinks to the bottom of a queue. Or a customer email forwarded into a channel with the information stripped out.
A chase email sent to the champion, who cannot pay it, while the real cause stays unexamined: a missing PO, a dispute or a delay in accounts payable.
A shared plan where only the vendor owns tasks. It is a to-do list the customer never signed up for, and it gives no warning when their side slips.
Presenting the retention number without its parts. It survives one question from anyone who has seen this before and loses the room after that.
The account that goes cold the moment it is marked lost. The data export is slow, the last conversation never happens, and a solvable loss becomes a customer who tells people how it ended.
A finished onboarding checklist attached to a customer who cannot say what changed.
The document the sponsor rewrites before forwarding it. Once they edit it, it stops sounding like them and you lose control of what their leadership reads.
A save that depends on which CSM owns the account. The same situation gets a different response every time because the play lives in one person's head.
The review that turns into a working session on the first account raised. Everyone leaves feeling it was useful, and most of the reads go unexamined.
A blanket increase sent to every account. It lands hardest on the accounts with a fragile sponsor or unproven value, and those are the ones that leave.
A forecast counted in logos. It reports a healthy quarter while the dollars come in short because accounts renewed smaller.
Negotiating price before value is agreed. With nothing on the other side of the scale, you argue about a number and lose.
At risk, low usage. It names a category, states no mechanism and implies no action, which makes it the most common line in a risk review and the least useful.
Starting the renewal plan from your own renewal date. The customer's notice date and budget cycle come first, and the decision may be made before you begin.
The promises made during the sale that never reached a system, found by the customer in the first month.
A save plan launched after the customer already chose a replacement, or one that opens with a discount before anyone has offered a fix.
A complete contact list for an account where nobody can name the decider.
A weekly update that lists activity. The manager learns nothing about outcomes and hears the bad news for the first time at the forecast call.
A survey score that sits in a spreadsheet. The detractor hears nothing back, and the promoter gets asked for a reference too often.
A summary that hides a risk until it is too big to hide. Leadership first hears about it when the renewal is lost.
A usage report that scolds. It lists unused seats as a failing, embarrasses a user in front of their boss and gets ignored.
Reaching renewal with a happy champion and no proof. When finance asks what the product delivered, nobody has the number.
Letting the loudest account become the theme. One customer's request gets reported as what customers want.
Answering whatever arrived last. The email from the signer who has waited since Monday sits under newer, smaller requests.
